summary: Describes the Certificate Request Message Format syntax and semantics, used to ask a Certification Authority, possibly via a Registration Authority, to produce an X.509 certificate. A request typically includes a public key and registration information. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: The Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF) defines the contents of a request for an X.509 certificate. It can include a certificate template, proof that the requester can use the matching private key, and extra registration information.

questions: what is proof of possession in pki
what is a certificate request message
subtitle: The message structure for requesting an X.509 certificate and demonstrating control of its key.

tldr.problem: Certificate enrollment needs a consistent way to describe the certificate being requested and, when required, show control of its private key.
tldr.mechanism: A CRMF message combines a certificate request template with optional proof-of-possession and registration information. A separate certificate request protocol carries the message and defines its surrounding procedures.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4211 replaces RFC 2511 and is updated by RFC 9045. It specifies a message format, not a complete enrollment protocol.

today: RFC 4211 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2511 and is updated by RFC 9045. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: A Message Format, Not a Protocol
sections.content:
CRMF is an object format for conveying a certificate request to a Certification Authority (CA), possibly through a Registration Authority (RA). A request typically includes a public key and registration information.

CRMF is not a stand-alone protocol. A separate Certificate Request Protocol defines how the message is carried, which algorithms are used, and which controls and registration information apply.
sections.plainLanguage: CRMF defines the information in a certificate request, not how the request travels to a certificate issuer. Another protocol supplies the transport and enrollment rules.

sections.title: The Certificate Request Message
sections.content:
A CertReqMsg contains a certReq certificate template, an optional popo proof-of-possession value, and optional regInfo attributes. The template describes requested certificate fields; not every field needs to be supplied.

The request identifier lets a requester match a request with its response. Registration information is supplementary, such as contact or billing information. A certificate request protocol decides what registration information is valid.
sections.plainLanguage: The message carries the certificate details being requested, optional proof of key possession, and optional supporting information. Its identifier helps match the request with a response.

sections.title: Proof of Possession
sections.content:
Proof-of-possession (POP) lets the requester demonstrate access to the private key that matches the public key in the request. Every certificate request protocol that uses CRMF must enforce POP by some means, either within CRMF or outside the message.

The message offers four choices: an RA's verification statement, a signature, a key-encipherment method, or a key-agreement method. Signature POP signs data that binds the identity and public key to the request. Other key types can use encrypted challenges or a message authentication code based on a shared or derived secret.
sections.plainLanguage: Proof-of-possession checks that the requester can use the private key matching the requested public key. The enrollment protocol chooses how that check is performed.

sections.title: The Certificate Template
sections.content:
The CertRequest contains an identifier, a certificate template, and optional controls. The template can include fields such as issuer, validity, subject, public key, and extensions. Some fields, including the serial number and signing algorithm, are assigned by the CA and must be omitted.

If the requester generates the key, the template must include its public key. A CA or RA may change requested fields other than the public key, so the requester must check the issued certificate to decide whether its contents are acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: The template lists the certificate fields the requester wants to supply. The issuer can set or change most requested fields, so the requester checks the certificate it receives.

sections.title: Controls and Registration Information
sections.content:
Controls affect how a request is handled but do not become certificate fields. The six controls defined here cover one-time identity information, an ongoing authenticator, publication preferences, private-key archiving, identification of an older certificate, and a key for encrypting the response.

The utf8Pairs registration-information control carries text name-value pairs. A separate certReq control lets an RA provide a revised template when it must change the request after the requester calculated proof-of-possession.
sections.plainLanguage: Controls give the issuer instructions or supporting information about the request. They can also carry a revised template when an RA needs to change certificate details.

sections.title: Password-Based Message Authentication
sections.content:
CRMF defines a password-based message authentication code for cases where the requester and CA or RA share a password. The process combines the password with a random salt, applies a one-way function repeatedly, and then calculates a message authentication code.

The salt should be at least 8 octets, and the iteration count must be at least 100. Implementations must support SHA-1 as the one-way function and HMAC-SHA1 as the message authentication code.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared password can help prove the requester's identity. CRMF adds a random salt and repeated hashing before calculating the check value.

sections.title: Protecting Enrollment Data and Keys
sections.content:
Enrollment can involve private keys and personal information. A certificate request protocol must protect subscriber-sensitive data through encryption or offline processing, and any out-of-band token delivery must match the risk the CA or RA accepts.

Without proof-of-possession, a certificate may incorrectly bind a public key to a name. Implementations must protect private keys and use high-entropy random values for keys, salts, and related cryptographic data. The RFC says remote generation should not be used for signing keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Enrollment messages may contain sensitive identity information and private keys, so the carrying protocol must protect them. Proof-of-possession helps ensure a certificate binds a name to a key the requester can use.
